title: Grammar in Context — The Deep Dive

pts: Deductive teaching gives the rule first, then examples; inductive (guided discovery) gives examples first and lets learners work out the rule.
Guided discovery tends to produce deeper processing and better retention for learners capable of the inference.
Match the choice to the structure's complexity and the learners' analytical readiness, not to habit.

blocks.x: Two ways to meet the present perfect

v: 40 minutes (two 20-minute halves, ideally with two parallel classes)
Six example sentences; a rule card

items: Deductive version. Show the rule card: ‘have/has + past participle for an action at an unspecified time before now, when the result or experience matters now’. Give two examples, then learners complete six sentences.
Inductive version. Show six example sentences without the rule. Ask: ‘Do we know when these things happened? Why does the speaker mention them now?’
Learners in pairs work out when the form is used and write their rule in one sentence.
Compare pairs’ rules with the rule card. Refine together.
Learners write two true sentences about their own experiences using the form.
If you taught both versions, compare how learners performed and what they remembered a week later.
Use a text (a short email home from someone travelling) as the source of examples for the inductive version.
Run the inductive version as a card sort: ‘time known’ versus ‘time not important’.
Support: highlight the verb forms in the examples.
Stretch: include a contrasting past simple sentence and ask learners to explain the difference.

lines: I’ve been to Mysuru three times.
She has lost her ID card, so she can’t enter the exam hall.
Have you ever eaten jackfruit?
We’ve finished the project. Here it is.
I went to Mysuru last Diwali. (contrast: time is known)
T: In sentence 1, do we know when?
Ss: No.
T: Is the speaker interested in the time, or in the experience?
S1: The experience.

blocks.x: When to choose which: deductive presentation suits complex rules, limited time and learners who expect explanation; inductive presentation suits patterns that can be seen in a handful of examples and classes that enjoy puzzles.

body: Purpose: to contrast the two routes. Content: two parallel flows. Left: a box ‘Rule’ → arrow → ‘Examples’ → arrow → ‘Practice’ (labelled ‘Deductive’). Right: ‘Examples’ → arrow → ‘Learners find the pattern’ → arrow → ‘Rule’ → arrow → ‘Practice’ (labelled ‘Inductive / guided discovery’). A small lightbulb icon beside the right-hand ‘Learners find the pattern’ box. Style: clean flowchart, two colours. Board version: two lines of boxes.

items: Google Forms (free). Build a short guided-discovery worksheet: examples at the top, then multiple-choice questions leading to the rule. Responses show which learners reached the rule unaided.

blocks.x: Write the example sentences on the board and cover the rule with a sheet of paper, revealing it only after learners have proposed their own.

pts: 'Focus on form' is a brief shift of attention to language within an otherwise meaning-focused task.
This differs from a 'focus on forms' syllabus, which teaches grammar points in isolation, one after another.
The brief, in-context correction is argued to be more durable than a standalone grammar lesson.

items: Run a meaning-focused speaking task (for example, planning a class trip in groups).
As you monitor, listen for a form that is causing real communication trouble for several learners, for example comparatives.
Pause the whole class briefly. Write one learner-produced sentence and its corrected form on the board.
Say it, ask the class to say it, and give one more example.
Return immediately to the task. The whole interruption should take less than three minutes.
Note which learners use the form correctly for the rest of the task.
Instead of pausing the class, give the focus to one group at a time as you visit.
Use a ‘language box’ in the corner of the board where you write quick forms throughout the lesson.
Support: leave the corrected form on the board for the rest of the task.
Stretch: ask stronger learners to find a second example in their own talk.

blocks.x: Focus on form versus focus on forms:

lines: Focus on forms: a lesson that teaches comparatives because they are next in the syllabus.
Focus on form: a brief turn to comparatives because learners need them right now to decide which trip is cheaper.

blocks.x: A brief turn during the task:

lines: S1: The zoo is more cheap than the museum.
T: [writes on board] cheap → cheaper. The zoo is cheaper. One syllable: add -er. The museum is… more interesting. OK, carry on!

body: Purpose: to show focus on form inside a meaning-focused task. Content: a long horizontal bar labelled ‘Meaning-focused task’. Partway along, a small dip in the bar labelled ‘2-minute focus on form’, after which the bar continues. Beneath, a contrasting bar made entirely of separate grammar blocks, labelled ‘Focus on forms: one form after another’. Style: simple bar diagram, one accent colour for the dip. Board version: a line with a small V-shaped dip.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic version). Use the text widget as a ‘language box’ that stays visible while learners continue the task.

blocks.x: Reserve a small box on the right-hand side of the board for quick forms. Learners copy it at the end of the lesson.

pts: Presentation–Practice–Production suits simple, single-form structures with a clear, controllable meaning.
For complex or recursive grammar, PPP's straight-line structure doesn't match how the item is actually acquired.
Dogme and task-based critiques argue for grammar that emerges from communication rather than preceding it.
points.who: Jim Scrivener; Scott Thornbury's Dogme critique

v: Pictures of daily routines; word cards

items: Presentation. Tell a short story about a friend’s daily routine using pictures, with the target structure (She gets up at six. She doesn’t eat breakfast.).
Check meaning. Ask concept-checking questions (point 7).
Practice. Learners match sentences to pictures, then drill them in pairs.
Production. Learners interview a partner about their routine and report back.
Second look. Ask learners to talk freely for two minutes about their weekend. Note whether the target form appears in freer talk and whether other forms (past, future) were needed but missing.
Use your notes to decide whether the next lesson follows PPP again or starts from a task.
Present through a short listening text rather than the teacher’s story.
Use a ‘test–teach–test’ order: start with the production task, teach what was missing, then repeat the task.
Support: extend the practice stage with picture prompts.
Stretch: at the production stage, learners compare their routine with a family member’s.

lines: A simple, single form with a clear meaning (present simple for routines; can for ability).
Learners at low levels who need a secure model before speaking.
Complex forms that develop gradually (articles, the present perfect).
Classes where learners already partly know the form and need to use it, not meet it.
Test: Plan a party in pairs. (Teacher notes: learners avoid going to.)
Teach: short focus on going to for plans.
Test: Plan a different party.

body: Purpose: to compare three lesson shapes. Content: three horizontal sequences of coloured blocks. First: P (Presentation) → P (Practice) → P (Production). Second: Test → Teach → Test. Third: Task → Report → Language focus. Each sequence has a short label beneath: ‘teacher leads first’, ‘diagnose first’, ‘communicate first’. Style: blocks in three colours, consistent across the three rows. Board version: three rows of letters and arrows.

items: Wordwall (free basic version). Use ‘Match up’ for the practice stage (sentences to pictures).

blocks.x: Picture cards drawn by learners themselves in the previous lesson: a morning routine in six pictures.

body: The label ‘PPP’ became widespread in teacher training in the 1980s and 1990s, but the sequence it describes is much older. Its critics, including Scott Thornbury and Luke Meddings (2009), argue that language does not arrive in learners’ heads in the order a syllabus presents it. Its defenders reply that a clear, secure model is exactly what beginners need. Both sides have a point, which is why this unit treats PPP as one tool among several.

pts: Instead of a pre-set grammar syllabus, the task itself generates the need for particular structures.
Grammar work happens in a 'language focus' stage after the task, addressing what learners actually struggled with.
This previews Tier II's task-based learning, where fluency and form are sequenced differently.
points.who: Rod Ellis, "Task-Based Language Learning and Teaching"

v: A task card (plan a one-day school trip on a budget); a recording or transcript of a proficient speaker doing the same task

items: Pre-task. Introduce the topic and the budget. Learners brainstorm places.
Task. In groups, learners plan the trip and agree a timetable. Monitor without correcting; note useful language and gaps.
Planning. Groups prepare to report their plan to the class.
Report. Groups present. Others ask one question each.
Language focus. Play or read the proficient speaker’s version. Learners find language for suggesting and agreeing (Why don’t we…? How about…? That’s a good idea, but…).
Learners practise the phrases briefly, then choose one they want to use next time.
Repeat the task a week later with a new budget to see whether the language is used.
Use learners’ own report transcripts (written from notes) for the language focus.
Support: provide a planning grid.
Stretch: add a constraint (one group member cannot walk far).

blocks.x: Language that often emerges as needed:

lines: Suggesting: Why don’t we…? How about going to…? We could…
Agreeing and disagreeing: Good idea. / I’m not sure. It might be too far.
Future plans: We’re going to leave at eight.

blocks.x: The task cycle (Willis 1996): pre-task → task → planning → report → language focus. The key difference from PPP is the order: communication comes first, and grammar work responds to what the task revealed.

body: Purpose: to show the order of stages. Content: a horizontal flow of five stages, with the first three grouped under a bracket labelled ‘meaning first’ and the last under a bracket labelled ‘form after’. Small icons: a lightbulb (pre-task), people talking (task), notebook (planning), microphone (report), magnifying glass (language focus). Style: clean flow, two colours. Board version: five words and arrows.

items: Phone voice recorder (built in). Record one group’s task with permission; use a short extract for the language-focus stage.

blocks.x: Your notes from monitoring are the language-focus material. Write three learner sentences and three improved versions on the board.

pts: Consciousness-raising tasks direct learners to notice a pattern in input, without requiring immediate production.
Noticing is treated as a necessary — though not sufficient — condition for acquisition.
These tasks work well as a light-touch alternative to explicit rule explanation.

v: A short text with several examples of a target form; highlighters

items: Learners read a short text for meaning (a gist question).
Give a noticing instruction: ‘Find every sentence with used to. Underline them.’
Ask questions that guide attention without giving a rule: ‘Is this about now or the past? Does it still happen?’
Pairs write what they think used to means.
Share, and agree a class version. Do not require learners to produce the form yet.
In a later lesson, return to the form in a speaking task.
Use a song or poem you have permission to use (see Unit 63), or a text learners wrote.
Compare with how the same idea is expressed in a home language.
Support: pre-highlight the first example.
Stretch: include one example of be used to and ask learners to explain why it is different.

lines: When my grandmother was young, she used to walk four kilometres to school. There were no buses then. She used to carry her books in a cloth bag. Her family didn’t have electricity, so she used to study by lamplight. Now she lives in the city and uses a smartphone.
T: Does she still walk to school?
Ss: No.
T: Did she do it once, or many times?
S1: Many times.

blocks.x: Noticing (Schmidt 1990): learners are more likely to acquire forms they have consciously noticed in input. A consciousness-raising task aims at noticing, not immediate production.

body: Purpose: to show noticing as a filter. Content: a stream of words flowing from left to right (the input). A magnifying glass in the middle picks out several highlighted words (used to) from the stream and drops them into a small box labelled ‘noticed’. The rest of the stream continues past. Style: simple, friendly; highlighted words in the accent colour. Board version: a line of words with some circled.

items: Google Docs (free). Share the text; learners use the highlighter tool to mark examples and add a comment with their rule.

blocks.x: Printed text and pencils. Learners underline and write their rule in the margin.

body: A consciousness-raising task has done its job if learners notice the pattern, even if they cannot yet use it. Resist the urge to follow every noticing task with immediate drilling. Give the form time and further encounters.

pts: Visual timelines make tense and aspect concrete, especially for perfect aspects that resist verbal explanation.
A drawn line with clear reference points often succeeds where a grammar-book rule fails.
Reuse the same visual convention across lessons so learners build a stable mental model.

v: A rope or a long line on the board; cards with now, yesterday, last year, for three years, since 2020

items: Draw a long line with an arrow. Mark NOW near the right.
Say a sentence about yourself: I have taught in this school for five years. Ask a learner to show where it begins and ends on the line.
Draw the timeline: a line starting five years ago and continuing to NOW.
Contrast with I taught in Hassan for three years (a closed box in the past).
Learners work in pairs: one says a true sentence, the other draws its timeline.
Keep the timelines on a poster and add to them each time a new tense is taught.
Make a human timeline: learners stand in the room holding time cards.
Use one colour for past, one for present, one for future throughout the year.
Support: provide sentences and let learners choose from three drawn timelines.
Stretch: add continuous aspect with wavy lines (I was cooking when the phone rang).

lines: I have lived in Mangaluru since 2019. → a line from 2019 to NOW, continuing.
I lived in Hassan from 2015 to 2019. → a closed box, finished before NOW.

blocks.x: A note on variety: speakers of Indian English sometimes use the progressive with stative verbs (I am knowing him for years). This is a recognized feature of the variety; in international and formal contexts, I have known him for years is more widely understood. Present it as a choice for audience, not a correction of identity.

body: Purpose: a reference poster for tense and aspect. Content: four horizontal timelines stacked vertically, each with a NOW marker. 1: past simple, a single cross in the past. 2: present perfect, a line from the past to NOW. 3: past continuous, a wavy line in the past crossed by a single cross. 4: going to future, an arrow from NOW to a cross in the future. Each has one short example sentence. Style: consistent symbols across all four, clean. Board version: as described.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers). Design a class timeline poster that learners can edit as they learn new tenses.

blocks.x: A washing line across the room with pegs and cards; learners physically place events on it.

pts: CCQs check understanding of meaning through targeted yes/no or short-answer questions.
'Do you understand?' invites a false yes; a CCQ like 'Is the action finished?' cannot be answered without real comprehension.
Write CCQs into the lesson plan in advance — they're hard to improvise well in the moment.

v: 10 minutes, used whenever new language is presented

items: After presenting a new form, do not ask ‘Do you understand?’
Ask two to four short concept-checking questions, prepared in advance, that can only be answered correctly if the meaning is understood.
If answers are wrong, re-present with a clearer example or timeline.
Ask learners to write one CCQ of their own for a new word or structure, and test a partner.
Use CCQs with true/false cards held up by the whole class, so everyone answers.
For young learners, use yes/no questions with pictures.
Support: give the answer options (yes/no).
Stretch: learners write CCQs that distinguish two confusable forms.

lines: She used to live in Hubballi. → Does she live there now? (No.) Did she live there for a long time? (Yes.)
You should see a doctor. → Is it a good idea? (Yes.) Is it a rule? (No.)
Can I borrow your pen? → Will I keep it? (No.) Will I give it back? (Yes.)

blocks.x: Why not ‘Do you understand?’: learners often say yes to avoid embarrassment, and some genuinely believe they understand when they do not.

body: Purpose: to show the contrast. Content: two speech-bubble scenes. Left: a teacher asks ‘Do you understand?’, a row of learners all say ‘Yes!’, and one thought bubble above a learner shows a question mark. Right: the teacher asks ‘Will I keep the pen?’; learners give different answers, and the teacher can see who understood. Style: friendly cartoon, not satirical. Board version: two bubbles.

items: Plickers (free basic version). Learners hold up cards to answer CCQs; the teacher scans the room with one phone and sees immediately who has understood.

blocks.x: Yes/no cards, or thumbs up and thumbs down held close to the chest so learners cannot copy each other.

points.sub: Not every error needs fixing now
pts: Some errors are a natural, temporary stage of interlanguage development and resolve with further exposure.
Others become fossilised — stable, resistant to correction, and requiring deliberate intervention.
Distinguishing the two prevents wasted correction effort on errors that would self-resolve.

v: Ten anonymous learner sentences from recent work; a class error log

items: Collect ten sentences with errors from recent speaking or writing. Include some errors many learners make and some made by only one or two.
Groups decide for each: ‘Is this a stage everyone goes through, or a stuck habit?’
Discuss as a class. Explain developmental errors (common, temporary, part of learning) and fossilized errors (stable, resistant, often long-standing).
Each learner finds one of their own recurring errors from their error log (Unit 8) and writes a personal action plan: when to check for it, how.
Revisit the plans after a month.
Compare an error learners made in Grade 5 work with their current work, where old notebooks are available.
Use a ‘grammar auction’: groups bid on sentences they think are correct.
Support: classify only five sentences.
Stretch: learners suggest why each error happens (overgeneralization, transfer, avoidance).

lines: Developmental: He goed home. (overgeneralizing -ed; tends to disappear as irregular forms are learned)
Possibly fossilized: She don’t like it. in an otherwise advanced learner, repeated for years despite correction
My error: missing s on third person verbs. When I check: every piece of writing, before I hand it in. How: I underline every he, she, it and check the verb.

body: Purpose: to show errors as stages. Content: a winding path from ‘first language’ at the left to ‘target language’ at the right. Along the path, small signposts labelled with typical developmental errors (He goed, Where you are going?). At one point, a small stone block sits on the path labelled ‘fossilized: needs a push’. Style: storybook landscape, gentle colours. Board version: a line with signposts and a block.

items: Google Sheets (free). A class error log shared with the teacher, one row per recurring error, with dates when it was noticed and when it was last seen.

blocks.x: A ruled error-log page at the back of each learner’s notebook, with columns: date, error, correct form, where I noticed it.

body: Take one learner’s writing from the start of the year and one from now. List the errors in each. Which errors have disappeared without explicit correction, and which have stayed despite it? The answer tells you where to focus your correction effort.

dek: Unit 6 of 100: moving past a purely linear Presentation-Practice-Production model toward noticing, task-driven grammar, and reading errors as development, not failure.

aims.x: This unit looks at grammar teaching through the lens of meaning. It compares rule-first and discovery-first approaches, places PPP alongside task-based and noticing-based alternatives, and treats learners’ errors as evidence of a developing system.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: choose between deductive and inductive presentation for a given structure and class;
use brief focus on form inside meaning-focused activities;
explain when PPP works well and when it does not;
plan a post-task language focus built on what learners actually needed;
design consciousness-raising tasks that lead learners to notice patterns;
use timelines and concept-checking questions to make meaning clear;
distinguish developmental errors from fossilized ones and respond differently.

why: Why this matters. Grammar taught only as rules to memorise rarely survives contact with real communication. Grammar taught through meaning and noticing tends to stick.

background.x: Few topics in language teaching have produced as much argument as grammar. For much of the twentieth century, grammar was the syllabus: learners worked through the verb tenses in order, one per unit, and a lesson was judged by whether the rule had been explained and practised. The communicative movement of the 1970s and 1980s reacted against this, and for a while some teachers avoided explicit grammar altogether. Research since then has settled into a more balanced view. Learners benefit from attention to form, but that attention works best when it is connected to meaning and when it arrives at the moment learners are ready to use it (Ellis 2003).

Noam Chomsky’s work gave the field a different reason to take grammar seriously. He argued that all children bring to language learning an innate capacity for grammar, which allows them to build a complex system from limited input (Chomsky 1965). Whether, and how far, that capacity remains available to adult second-language learners is still debated, and Unit 86 returns to the question. For the classroom teacher, the lasting point is that learners are not empty containers for rules. They are active builders of their own grammar, forming and testing hypotheses all the time.

That view changes how errors look. When a learner says I goed to the market, she is not ignoring the rule; she is applying one (add -ed for the past) more widely than English allows. Larry Selinker (1972) called the learner’s developing system an interlanguage: a real, rule-governed system in its own right, neither the first language nor the target language. Teaching grammar well means working with that system, not just correcting its outputs.

In multilingual classrooms, learners’ other grammars are part of the picture too. A Kannada or Hindi speaker brings a language in which the verb usually comes at the end of the clause, and in which postpositions follow nouns rather than prepositions preceding them. Comparing structures across languages, briefly and without judgement, often helps learners see what is distinctive about English.

items: Rule articulation. After a guided-discovery lesson, ask learners to write the rule in their own words. Clear, accurate rules show understanding; confused ones show where to re-teach.
Use in freer tasks. Record whether target forms appear in a speaking task a week after teaching. Presence in free use is stronger evidence of learning than accuracy in a gap-fill.
CCQ responses. Track the proportion of the class answering CCQs correctly (for example with Plickers) across several lessons.
Error log review. Once a month, review learners’ error logs and note which errors have disappeared and which persist.
Do you tend to present grammar deductively or inductively? Is that a choice or a habit?
When did you last interrupt a speaking task to focus briefly on form? What happened?
Which of your learners’ errors are developmental, and which may be fossilized? How do you decide?
How do you handle features of Indian English grammar that differ from the textbook model?
What would a lesson look like if the grammar came after the task rather than before?

terms.def: A grammatical category showing how an action or state is viewed in time, for example as complete or in progress; English marks progressive aspect (is writing) and perfect aspect (has written).
A short question that checks whether learners have understood the meaning of new language, such as ‘Is he still at school?’ after he used to go to school.
Activities that help learners notice and work out a grammatical feature for themselves, rather than practising it, often by examining examples and forming a rule.
Teaching that presents a rule first and then asks learners to apply it in examples; contrast inductive teaching, in which learners work out the rule.
An error that reflects a natural stage in learning a language, such as goed for went, rather than interference from the first language.
Briefly drawing learners’ attention to language forms as they arise during meaning-focused activity, such as a task or discussion (Long 1991). It contrasts with focus on forms.
Teaching language forms as the main content of lessons, one by one, often through presentation and practice of a pre-selected grammar point (Long 1991). It contrasts with focus on form.
The persistence of certain errors in a learner’s language despite further exposure and teaching, such as a stable He go in an otherwise advanced speaker (Selinker 1972).
A way of teaching in which learners work out a rule or pattern from examples, guided by the teacher’s questions, rather than being told the rule first.
Teaching in which learners meet examples first and work out the rule or pattern themselves, as opposed to deductive teaching, which begins with the rule.
The developing language system of a second language learner, which has its own rules and differs from both the first language and the target language (Selinker 1972).
Conscious attention to a feature of the input, such as a verb ending, which is argued to be necessary for it to be learnt (Schmidt 1990).
Applying a rule beyond its proper range, as in goed or childs; such errors show that a learner is actively building a system rather than simply copying.
A lesson sequence in which the teacher presents a language item, learners practise it in controlled activities, and then use it more freely in production.
The central phase of a task-based lesson, in which learners do the task, plan a report and present it to the class (Willis 1996). It is preceded by a pre-task and followed by a language focus.
A lesson sequence in which learners first attempt a task to reveal what they know, the teacher then teaches the language they need, and learners attempt a similar task again.
A line diagram showing past, present and future, used to clarify the time reference of verb forms, such as the difference between the past simple and present perfect.
